q: After a vasectomy, a man's semen contains no sperm, yet its volume is only slightly reduced. Which explanation accounts for this?
o: Most of the fluid enters past the cut, from the seminal vesicles and prostate
Most of the fluid comes from the seminiferous tubules, which keep secreting
Most of the fluid is made in the epididymis, which lies past the cut
Most of the fluid comes from the bulbourethral glands, which drain into the ductus
w: Two steps. (1) A vasectomy cuts the ductus (vas) deferens, so sperm from the seminiferous tubules and epididymis cannot pass. (2) The seminal vesicles (about 60% of semen) join the tract at the ejaculatory duct, and the prostate surrounds the urethra; both lie downstream of the cut, so their fluid still makes up most of the semen.

n.1: The seminiferous tubules produce sperm and lie upstream of the cut, so nothing from them reaches the ejaculate.
n.2: The epididymis lies before the ductus deferens, upstream of the cut, and it matures and stores sperm rather than making most of the semen fluid.
n.3: The bulbourethral glands add a small amount of mucus, and they drain into the urethra, not the ductus deferens.

q: Place the structures in the order sperm pass through them, starting where sperm are produced and ending where they leave the body during ejaculation.
o: Epididymis
Ejaculatory duct
Spongy (penile) urethra
Prostatic urethra
Ductus (vas) deferens
Seminiferous tubules
w: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, mature and are stored in the epididymis, travel through the ductus deferens (via the inguinal canal), enter the ejaculatory duct where the seminal vesicle duct joins, then pass through the prostatic urethra inside the prostate and finally the spongy urethra of the penis (the short membranous urethra lies between those two). Mnemonic: SEVEn UP.

q: In a man, Sertoli cells increase their secretion of inhibin as sperm production rises. Which hormonal change follows most directly from the higher inhibin level?
o: Higher GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus
Lower testosterone secretion by the Sertoli cells
Lower FSH secretion by the anterior pituitary
Lower LH secretion by the anterior pituitary
w: Inhibin from Sertoli cells is a negative-feedback signal that suppresses FSH release from the anterior pituitary, slowing spermatogenesis. Testosterone is the main feedback signal that holds LH in check.

n.0: Inhibin is an inhibitory feedback signal, so it would not raise GnRH output.
n.1: Sertoli cells do not secrete testosterone; Leydig cells do, under LH control.
n.3: LH is held in check mainly by testosterone feedback; inhibin targets FSH.

q: The testes sit in the scrotum, outside the pelvic cavity, instead of inside the abdomen. Which statement best explains why this position matters for sperm production?
o: Sperm mature inside the scrotal sac before they move into the epididymis
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius above core body temperature
Leydig cells stop secreting testosterone when held at core body temperature
w: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules works best at about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature, so the scrotum holds the testes outside the body cavity.

n.0: Sperm mature in the epididymis after leaving the seminiferous tubules, not in the scrotal sac before reaching it.
n.2: The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the body core, not warmer.
n.3: The position matters for spermatogenesis in the tubules; testosterone secretion by Leydig cells is not what the cooler setting protects.

q: A normal human sperm cell fertilizes a normal secondary oocyte. Which statement about the chromosomes carried by that sperm is correct?
o: It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, carrying either an X or a Y chromosome
It is diploid, carrying 46 chromosomes including one X and one Y
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, and the egg's chromosome sets the child's sex
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, each sperm carrying an X chromosome
w: Meiosis makes sperm haploid (n = 23). Each sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm determines the child's sex; the egg carries an X. Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).

n.1: Gametes are haploid; 46 chromosomes is the diploid number restored at fertilization.
n.2: The egg carries an X in every case, so it is the sperm's X or Y that sets the child's sex.
n.3: It is the egg that carries an X in every case; sperm carry either an X or a Y.

q: In a sample of testicular tissue, 25 primary spermatocytes each complete both meiotic divisions normally. How many spermatids are produced in total? Enter a whole number.

tr.25: One gamete per cell, as in oogenesis.
tr.50: Counting meiosis I only (2 secondary spermatocytes per primary spermatocyte).

w: Each primary spermatocyte goes through meiosis I (giving 2 secondary spermatocytes) and meiosis II (giving 4 haploid spermatids). Unlike oogenesis, which yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies, no cells are lost as polar bodies. 25 x 4 = 100 spermatids.

q: Which statements about the hormonal control of the testes are correct? Select all that apply.
o: FSH and testosterone together stimulate spermatogenesis via Sertoli cells.
FSH from the posterior pituitary acts on the Sertoli cells.
Testosterone raises GnRH output by positive feedback on the hypothalamus.
LH stimulates interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone.
Leydig cells line the seminiferous tubules and nourish developing sperm.
Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH release.
w: LH acts on Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. FSH, together with testosterone, acts through the Sertoli cells to drive spermatogenesis. Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH.

n.1: FSH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the posterior pituitary.
n.2: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH and LH.
n.4: Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells, line the tubules and nourish developing sperm; Leydig cells sit between the tubules.

q: A semen analysis shows sperm with normal heads and tails but abnormal midpieces. Which function would be most directly impaired in these sperm?
o: Releasing enzymes that digest the oocyte's outer layers
Supplying the ATP that powers movement of the tail
Storing the fructose that sperm use as an energy source
Delivering 23 chromosomes to the oocyte at fertilization
w: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP to power the flagellum. A defective midpiece leaves the tail short of energy, reducing motility.

n.0: The penetrating enzymes sit in the acrosome on the head, which is normal here.
n.2: Fructose is supplied in seminal vesicle fluid; it is not stored in the sperm's midpiece.
n.3: The chromosomes are in the nucleus of the head, which is normal here.

q: After ovulation, the fimbriae sweep the secondary oocyte into the uterine tube. In a typical pregnancy, where does fertilization of the oocyte take place?
o: In the ampulla of the uterine tube
In the ruptured follicle of the ovary
In the functional layer of the endometrium
In the cervical canal of the uterus
w: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer portion of the uterine tube. Cilia and peristalsis then move the developing embryo to the uterus, where it implants in the endometrium.

n.1: The oocyte leaves the ovary at ovulation; the ruptured follicle then becomes the corpus luteum.
n.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants about a week later, not where fertilization occurs.
n.3: Sperm pass through the cervix on the way up; fertilization happens farther along, in the uterine tube.

q: In a typical 28-day cycle, the dominant follicle releases a secondary oocyte around day 14. Which hormonal event directly causes this ovulation?
o: A sharp fall in estrogen from the follicles
A surge of FSH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of LH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of progesterone from the corpus luteum
w: High estrogen from the dominant (Graafian) follicle triggers the LH surge from the anterior pituitary, and the LH surge causes the follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte.

n.0: Estrogen is high, not falling, just before ovulation; high estrogen is what triggers the LH surge.
n.1: FSH stimulates follicle growth earlier in the follicular phase; the LH surge is what causes ovulation.
n.3: The corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, so its progesterone cannot trigger ovulation.

q: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does the corpus luteum mainly secrete, and what is its main effect on the uterus?
o: Progesterone, which keeps the endometrium in its secretory state
Estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium after menstruation
FSH, which prepares the endometrium for implantation
Progesterone, which stimulates contractions of the myometrium
w: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone (plus some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thickened, secretory endometrium and relaxes the myometrium, preparing the uterus for implantation.

n.1: Rebuilding the endometrium in the proliferative phase is driven by estrogen from growing follicles before ovulation.
n.2: FSH is an anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates follicles; the corpus luteum does not secrete it.
n.3: Progesterone relaxes the myometrium; oxytocin is the hormone that stimulates uterine contractions.

q: A new mother notices that milk begins flowing from her breasts within seconds after her infant starts to suckle. Which hormone, from which gland, causes this milk ejection?
o: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary
Oxytocin from the anterior pituitary
Prolactin from the posterior pituitary
w: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection (let-down). Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production.

n.1: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production, not the rapid ejection of milk.
n.2: Oxytocin causes ejection, but it is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.
n.3: Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone, and it governs milk production rather than ejection.

q: A home pregnancy test detects a hormone in urine shortly after a blastocyst implants. Which statement correctly identifies this hormone and its role in early pregnancy?
o: hCG from the mother's anterior pituitary, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
Progesterone from the corpus luteum, which keeps the endometrium intact
hCG from the embryo's trophoblast, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
LH from the mother's anterior pituitary, which triggers implantation
w: Pregnancy tests detect hCG, secreted by the trophoblast of the implanted blastocyst (later the placenta). hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive so it keeps secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium.

n.0: hCG is made by the embryo's trophoblast, not by the mother's pituitary.
n.1: Progesterone does maintain the endometrium, but home pregnancy tests detect hCG, not progesterone.
n.3: LH triggers ovulation, not implantation, and it is not the hormone pregnancy tests detect.

q: Place these events of a typical 28-day ovarian and uterine cycle in order, starting with day 1 of the cycle.
o: Estrogen from growing follicles rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase)
The functional layer of the endometrium is shed (menstrual phase)
An LH surge causes the dominant follicle to release a secondary oocyte
The corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone levels fall
Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrium secretory
w: Days 1 to 5: menstrual phase, as the functional layer is shed. Days 6 to 14: FSH-stimulated follicles secrete estrogen that rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase). About day 14: high estrogen triggers the LH surge and ovulation. Days 15 to 28: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and the endometrium is secretory. Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates near the end of the cycle, progesterone falls, and menstruation begins again.

q: Which statement correctly describes the cell that the ovary releases at ovulation and the stage its meiosis has reached?
o: A mature ovum that completed meiosis II before leaving the ovary
A secondary oocyte that completes meiosis II if it is fertilized
A primary oocyte that completes meiosis I in the uterine tube
A secondary oocyte that completed meiosis II at the LH surge
w: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from before birth until puberty. Each cycle, one completes meiosis I just before ovulation, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte is released and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm fertilizes it.

n.0: Meiosis II is not finished before ovulation; it is completed after fertilization.
n.2: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation, so the released cell is already a secondary oocyte.
n.3: The LH surge is followed by completion of meiosis I, not meiosis II; meiosis II waits for fertilization.

q: Six primary oocytes and six primary spermatocytes complete meiosis normally, and each oocyte is fertilized so that meiosis II finishes. How many ova and how many sperm result in total?
o: 6 ova and 24 sperm
6 ova and 12 sperm
24 ova and 24 sperm
12 ova and 24 sperm
w: Two steps. (1) Oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally, so each primary oocyte yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies: 6 x 1 = 6 ova. (2) Spermatogenesis yields 4 sperm per primary spermatocyte: 6 x 4 = 24 sperm.

n.1: This counts 2 sperm per spermatocyte, which stops after meiosis I; meiosis II gives 4 per spermatocyte.
n.2: This treats oogenesis like spermatogenesis; polar bodies are not functional ova, so each oocyte gives 1 ovum.
n.3: This counts the first polar body as a second ovum; polar bodies degenerate and are not ova.

q: To slow preterm labor, a patient is given a drug that blocks oxytocin receptors in the uterus. The activity of which part of the uterus is this drug intended to reduce?
o: Myometrium, the smooth muscle layer
Cervix, the narrow lower neck
Endometrium, the glandular lining
Perimetrium, the outer serous layer
w: Two steps. (1) Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary stimulates uterine contractions in labor. (2) Those contractions come from the myometrium, the smooth muscle layer of the uterine wall. Blocking oxytocin receptors aims to quiet the myometrium.

n.1: The cervix is the lower neck that opens into the vagina; the contractions oxytocin drives come from the myometrium of the uterine wall.
n.2: The endometrium is the lining where implantation occurs and that is shed in menstruation; it does not generate labor contractions.
n.3: The perimetrium is the thin outer covering of the uterus; it does not produce the contractions of labor.

q: A 56-year-old woman has gone through menopause, and her ovaries no longer contain functioning follicles. Which pattern of hormone levels is expected in her blood?
o: High estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with high FSH and LH
Low estrogen with high progesterone and low FSH
w: Two steps. (1) With the follicles exhausted, the ovaries make little estrogen and progesterone. (2) Those hormones normally exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so without them FSH and LH rise.

n.0: Without functioning follicles the ovaries cannot keep estrogen and progesterone high.
n.1: Falling ovarian hormones remove negative feedback, so FSH and LH rise rather than fall.
n.3: Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation, so it is low after menopause; FSH is high.

q: Which events occur during the luteal phase of a 28-day cycle in which pregnancy does not occur? Select all that apply.
o: An LH surge triggers rupture of the dominant follicle.
The corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls.
FSH stimulates the growth of a dominant follicle.
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone.
The endometrium is in its secretory phase.
The functional layer of the endometrium is shed.
w: The luteal phase (about days 15 to 28) follows ovulation: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, the endometrium is secretory, and with no embryo making hCG the corpus luteum degenerates late in the phase, so progesterone falls.

n.0: The LH surge and follicle rupture occur at ovulation, about day 14, which ends the follicular phase.
n.2: FSH-driven growth of the dominant follicle happens in the follicular phase, before ovulation.
n.5: Shedding of the functional layer is the menstrual phase (days 1 to 5), which follows the fall in progesterone.

q: About a week after fertilization, the developing human implants in the endometrium of the uterus. Which stage implants, and how is it correctly described?
o: Blastocyst, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
Morula, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Blastocyst, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Morula, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
w: Development runs zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation, embryo (to week 8), fetus (week 9 to birth). The blastocyst implants about 6 to 7 days after fertilization, and its trophoblast later forms part of the placenta and secretes hCG.

n.0: Blastocyst is the right stage, but it is hollow (a fluid-filled cavity ringed by trophoblast); the solid ball made by cleavage is the morula.
n.1: A hollow ball with a trophoblast layer is the blastocyst; the morula is a solid ball with no cavity or trophoblast, and it comes first.
n.3: The morula is the solid ball formed by cleavage, but it develops into a blastocyst before implantation; the morula does not implant.

q: A student is sorting the body's defenses into categories for a study guide. Which of the following belongs in the first line of defense, the external barriers?
o: Complement proteins that lyse microbes
Interferons released by virus-infected cells
Lysozyme in tears and saliva
Neutrophils that engulf bacteria in the tissues
w: The first line of defense is the external barriers: intact skin, mucous membranes and mucus, cilia, stomach acid, and secretions such as tears and saliva that contain the antibacterial enzyme lysozyme.

n.0: Complement proteins circulate in the blood plasma, a second-line defense.
n.1: Interferons act inside the body after a virus has infected cells, a second-line defense.
n.3: Neutrophils are internal phagocytes, part of the second line of defense.

q: Within hours of bacteria entering a cut on the hand, white blood cells pour into the injured tissue. Which phagocytes typically arrive first and in the largest numbers?
o: Neutrophils
Natural killer cells
Dendritic cells
Macrophages
w: Neutrophils are the first phagocytes to arrive in large numbers at a site of bacterial infection. Monocytes follow and become macrophages.

n.1: NK cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells; they are not the phagocytes that clear bacteria from a wound.
n.2: Dendritic cells are phagocytes best known for presenting antigen to T cells; they are not the first wave that floods infected tissue.
n.3: Macrophages develop from monocytes that arrive after the neutrophils.

q: After a splinter pierces the skin, mast cells near the wound release histamine. Which effect of histamine directly produces the redness and swelling around the splinter?
o: Release of pyrogens that reset the hypothalamus
Vasodilation with decreased capillary permeability
Vasodilation with increased capillary permeability
Vasoconstriction with decreased capillary permeability
w: Histamine dilates local blood vessels (more blood flow: redness and heat) and makes capillaries leakier (fluid moves into the tissue: swelling). These changes also help phagocytes reach the site.

n.0: Pyrogens resetting the hypothalamus cause fever, a body-wide response, not local redness and swelling.
n.1: Vasodilation explains the redness, but the swelling needs increased permeability so fluid leaks into the tissue.
n.3: Vasoconstriction would reduce blood flow and redness; histamine dilates vessels.

q: A cell infected with a virus secretes proteins that diffuse to nearby cells and help those cells resist infection by the virus. Which innate defense does this describe?
o: Antibodies from plasma cells
Interferons
Histamine from mast cells
Complement proteins
w: Interferons are made by virus-infected cells and protect neighboring cells, an innate second-line defense.

n.0: Antibodies come from plasma cells in the adaptive response, not from the infected cell itself.
n.2: Histamine from mast cells drives inflammation; it does not help neighboring cells resist a virus.
n.3: Complement proteins circulate in plasma, lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis; infected cells do not secrete them to protect their neighbors.

q: Which cell destroys virus-infected cells and tumor cells without needing prior exposure to a specific antigen, making it part of innate rather than adaptive immunity?
o: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cell
Natural killer cell
Helper (CD4) T cell
Plasma cell
w: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate defenders that kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior exposure to the antigen.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells also kill infected cells, but they must first be activated by a specific antigen, so they are adaptive.
n.2: Helper T cells coordinate the adaptive response; they do not kill cells directly.
n.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies in the adaptive humoral response.

q: A patient with a bacterial infection develops a moderate fever. Which statement best describes how the fever arises and how it helps the body?
o: Histamine resets the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat activates memory cells
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the pituitary set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, giving an antigen-specific adaptive defense
w: Fever is an innate, nonspecific second-line defense. Pyrogens released during infection reset the temperature set point in the hypothalamus, and a moderate rise in body temperature inhibits pathogens.

n.0: Pyrogens, not histamine, reset the set point; histamine drives local inflammation, and memory cells belong to adaptive immunity.
n.2: The body's temperature set point is in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.
n.3: Fever is innate and nonspecific; it does not target one antigen the way adaptive immunity does.

q: Place these events of the inflammatory response to a contaminated skin wound in order, starting with the first.
o: Mast cells release histamine and other mediators
Phagocytes squeeze out of capillaries and move toward the site
Local blood vessels dilate and capillaries become leakier
Phagocytes engulf and destroy the bacteria
Tissue is injured and bacteria enter the wound
w: Injury lets bacteria in. Mast cells (and basophils) release histamine, which causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, producing redness, heat, swelling and pain. Phagocytes then leave the capillaries (diapedesis) and follow chemical signals to the site (chemotaxis), where they engulf the invaders (phagocytosis).

q: After a car accident, a patient's ruptured spleen is surgically removed. Which normal function is most directly lost along with the spleen?
o: Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the intestine
Filtering lymph before it returns to the bloodstream
Maturing T lymphocytes before they enter circulation
Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
w: The spleen, the largest lymphoid organ, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old or damaged red blood cells and platelets and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

n.0: Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats; the spleen has no part in fat absorption.
n.1: Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood.
n.2: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the spleen.

q: Lymph collected from the left arm, the abdomen and both legs must return to the bloodstream. By which route does this lymph re-enter the blood?
o: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the superior vena cava
w: The thoracic duct drains most of the body, including both legs, the abdomen and the left arm, into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax.

n.1: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax, not the left arm or the legs.
n.2: The thoracic duct joins the venous system on the left side, at the left subclavian vein.
n.3: The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, not directly into the superior vena cava.

q: Lymphatic vessels have no pump like the heart, yet lymph from the legs still moves steadily up toward the veins of the upper chest. Which mechanism keeps it moving one way?
o: Rhythmic pumping by the lymph nodes, with valves
Pressure from the right ventricle, with valves
Skeletal muscle and breathing movements, with valves
Suction as the spleen filters the lymph, with valves
w: Lymph is moved by the squeezing of skeletal muscles and the pressure changes of breathing; valves in the lymphatic vessels keep the flow one-way toward the subclavian veins.

n.0: Lymph nodes filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages; they do not contract to pump it along.
n.1: The right ventricle pumps blood out to the lungs; it gives no push to lymph, which drifts through low-pressure vessels toward the veins.
n.3: The spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it does not draw lymph through the lymphatic vessels.

q: Which of the following are part of the second line of defense, the internal nonspecific (innate) defenses? Select all that apply.
o: Plasma cells secreting antibodies
Complement proteins
Fever
Cytotoxic T cells
Natural killer cells
Lysozyme in saliva
w: Second-line defenses act inside the body and are nonspecific: phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation, fever, complement proteins and interferons.

n.0: Antibody-secreting plasma cells belong to the third line, adaptive humoral immunity.
n.3: Cytotoxic T cells are antigen-specific lymphocytes of the third line, adaptive cell-mediated immunity.
n.5: Lysozyme in saliva and tears is a first-line, external barrier defense.

q: After several axillary lymph nodes are removed during breast cancer surgery, a patient develops lasting swelling of the arm on that side. Which lymphatic function best explains the swelling?
o: Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood
Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the villi
Filtering lymph to trap microbes before it reaches the blood
w: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid (lymph) and return it to the blood. Removing the axillary nodes disrupts drainage from the arm, so fluid builds up in the tissues.

n.0: Filtering blood and removing old red blood cells is a function of the spleen, not the axillary lymph nodes.
n.2: Lacteals absorb fats in the intestinal villi; they do not drain the arm.
n.3: The nodes do filter lymph, but losing that filter would raise infection risk; the swelling comes from fluid that is no longer drained.

q: During a humoral immune response to a bacterial toxin, which cells secrete large amounts of antibodies that circulate in the blood and lymph?
o: Cytotoxic T cells that recognize the toxin
Plasma cells derived from activated B cells
Helper T cells that coordinate the response
Memory B cells that persist after infection
w: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells, which wait for a later exposure.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly in cell-mediated immunity; they do not make antibodies.
n.2: Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells, but they do not secrete antibodies.
n.3: Memory B cells give a faster response on re-exposure; the antibody-secreting cells are plasma cells.

q: Both B and T lymphocytes arise from stem cells in red bone marrow. Where does each type of lymphocyte complete its maturation before it can respond to antigens?
o: T cells in the thymus; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the lymph nodes; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the thymus; B cells in the spleen
T cells in red bone marrow; B cells in the thymus
w: T cells mature in the thymus (T for thymus), and B cells mature in red bone marrow. These are the two primary lymphoid organs.

n.1: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs that house mature lymphocytes; T cells mature in the thymus.
n.2: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes respond to antigens; B cells mature in red bone marrow.
n.3: This reverses the two sites: T cells mature in the thymus and B cells in red bone marrow.

q: In advanced HIV infection, both antibody production and cell-mediated killing become weak. Destruction of which cell type best explains the failure of both responses?
o: Natural killer cells
B lymphocytes
Helper (CD4) T cells
Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
w: Two steps. (1) HIV destroys helper (CD4) T cells. (2) Helper T cells normally activate both B cells (antibody response) and cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated response), so losing them weakens both arms of adaptive immunity.

n.0: NK cells are innate; losing them would not explain the failure of both adaptive responses.
n.1: Losing B cells would reduce antibodies but not cell-mediated killing; HIV targets helper T cells.
n.3: Losing cytotoxic T cells would weaken cell-mediated killing but would not explain the weak antibody response; HIV targets CD4 cells.

q: A newborn is protected against several infections for the first few months of life by antibodies received from the mother before birth. Which antibody class provides this protection?
o: IgA
IgM
IgE
IgG
w: IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, giving the fetus naturally acquired passive immunity that fades over weeks to months after birth.

n.0: IgA reaches the infant in breast milk after birth, not across the placenta before birth.
n.1: IgM is a large pentamer that does not cross the placenta; it is the first antibody made in a primary response.
n.2: IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy and parasite defense; it does not cross the placenta.

q: A child receives a booster dose of a vaccine one year after the first dose. Compared with the response to the first dose, how does the response to the booster differ?
o: Faster and stronger, mainly IgM, because memory cells already exist
Slower and weaker, because leftover antibodies block the antigen
Faster and stronger, mainly IgG, because memory cells already exist
Similar in speed, mainly IgM, because plasma cells must form again
w: The first dose triggers a primary response (a lag of days, mainly IgM) and leaves memory cells. On re-exposure, the memory cells drive a secondary response that is faster, stronger and longer lasting and is dominated by IgG. This is why booster doses work.

n.0: Faster and stronger is right, but the secondary response is mainly IgG; IgM dominates the primary response.
n.1: Memory cells make the secondary response faster and stronger, not slower and weaker.
n.3: Memory cells make the secondary response faster, and IgG rather than IgM dominates it.

q: Place these steps of a humoral (antibody-mediated) response to a newly encountered bacterial antigen in order, starting with the first.
o: A helper T cell recognizes the displayed antigen and is activated
Plasma cells secrete antibodies that bind the antigen
The B cell divides and differentiates into plasma cells and memory cells
The helper T cell releases cytokines that activate a matching B cell
A dendritic cell engulfs the bacterium and displays its antigen on MHC proteins
w: An antigen-presenting cell (here a dendritic cell) shows antigen fragments on MHC proteins. A helper T cell that recognizes the antigen is activated and releases cytokines that activate a B cell with a matching receptor. The B cell multiplies into plasma cells (which secrete antibodies against the antigen) and memory B cells.

q: Minutes after a bee sting, a student who was sensitized by an earlier sting develops hives and wheezing. Which antibody, bound to which cells, triggers this reaction?
o: IgE bound to neutrophils and macrophages
IgA bound to cells of mucous membranes
IgG bound to mast cells and basophils
IgE bound to mast cells and basophils
w: Allergy and anaphylaxis are IgE-mediated. IgE made after the first sting binds to mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen binds that IgE and the cells release histamine and other mediators. Severe anaphylaxis is treated with epinephrine.

n.0: IgE is right, but it binds mast cells and basophils, the histamine-releasing cells, not phagocytes.
n.1: IgA protects mucous membranes in secretions; it does not trigger allergic reactions.
n.2: IgG is the main antibody of secondary responses in the blood; the antibody that arms mast cells in allergy is IgE.

q: A hiker bitten by a rattlesnake is treated with antivenom, a preparation of ready-made antibodies against the venom. Which type of immunity does the antivenom provide?
o: Artificially acquired passive immunity, immediate but temporary
Artificially acquired passive immunity, immediate and long-lasting
Artificially acquired active immunity, slow to start but long-lasting
Naturally acquired passive immunity, immediate but temporary
w: Antivenom delivers ready-made antibodies by injection: artificial (a medical intervention) and passive (the hiker's own immune system did not make them). Passive immunity works at once but fades within weeks to months and leaves no memory cells.

n.1: Passive immunity creates no memory cells, so it is temporary rather than long-lasting.
n.2: Active immunity requires the body to make its own antibodies, as after a vaccine; antivenom supplies them ready-made.
n.3: Natural passive immunity comes from the mother (IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk), not from an injection.

q: Several weeks after a kidney transplant, the recipient's immune system begins attacking the donor organ. Which cells directly kill the transplanted kidney cells?
o: Helper (CD4) T cells
Antibody-secreting plasma cells
Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
Regulatory T cells
w: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells of cell-mediated immunity directly kill virus-infected cells, cancer cells and transplanted cells.

n.0: Helper T cells coordinate the attack through cytokines but do not kill the cells themselves.
n.1: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they do not make direct cell-to-cell kills.
n.3: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses; they would dampen rejection rather than carry it out.

q: Before helper T cells can respond to a new pathogen, other cells must display fragments of the pathogen's antigens on MHC proteins. Which cells perform this antigen presentation?
o: Helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells
Mast cells and basophils
Dendritic cells and macrophages
Plasma cells and natural killer cells
w: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells) take in antigens and display fragments on MHC proteins so that T cells can recognize them.

n.0: T cells are the cells that recognize presented antigen; they are not the antigen-presenting cells.
n.1: Mast cells and basophils release histamine in inflammation and allergy; they are not antigen-presenting cells.
n.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and NK cells kill infected cells; neither presents antigen to T cells.

q: Which of the following give a person passive immunity? Select all that apply.
o: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta to a fetus
Recovery from a natural chickenpox infection
An injection of tetanus immune globulin after a wound
IgA received by an infant through breast milk
An mRNA vaccine against a respiratory virus
A tetanus toxoid vaccine given as a booster
w: Passive immunity means receiving ready-made antibodies: naturally (IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk) or artificially (immune globulin, antivenom, antitoxin). Vaccines and infections make the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells, which is active immunity.

n.1: Having the infection gives naturally acquired active immunity.
n.4: Vaccines, including mRNA vaccines, give artificially acquired active immunity.
n.5: A toxoid vaccine stimulates the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells: artificially acquired active immunity.

q: Which of the following disorders results from the immune system attacking the body's own tissues?
o: Osteoarthritis of the knees
Hay fever triggered by pollen
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis
w: In autoimmune disease the immune system attacks self antigens. In rheumatoid arthritis it attacks the synovial membranes of the joints. Other examples include type 1 diabetes, lupus, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease.

n.0: Osteoarthritis is wear-and-tear breakdown of articular cartilage, not an immune attack; rheumatoid arthritis is the autoimmune joint disease.
n.1: Hay fever is an IgE-mediated allergy (hypersensitivity) to a foreign antigen, pollen, not an attack on self tissue.
n.2: Type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance; it is type 1 diabetes in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells.
